1635.prule: No fixed stress rule is stated by any reachable source; the prosodic type itself is contested. Ferraz (1979: 25) and Schang (2003: 87-88) analyse Santome as a stress language (no phonologically significant tone; stress on the final, penultimate or antepenultimate syllable, largely continuing the Portuguese etymon, verbs final-stressed), whereas Maurer (1995, 2008) analyses it as a two-tone (H/L) language. Hagemeijer 2013's survey text reports the dispute neutrally, but in the same work's structure dataset (APiCS 35-120) he codes Santome 'Simple tone system, for lexical and grammatical distinctions', confidence 'Very certain', with tonal minimal pairs from Maurer 2008 (bóbó 'idiot' vs bóbò 'mulatto', kúlù 'unripe' vs kúlú 'dark', lala LL 'grater' vs lálá HH 'to grate'). Bandeira 2017 rejects Maurer's tonal analysis ('não é possível propor que o santome apresenta um sistema tonal'), floats pitch accent, treats Santome as having word accent on one of the last three syllables, and calls for further study. Two reachable open texts thus take irreconcilable positions (Hagemeijer/Maurer: tone; Bandeira/Ferraz/Schang: stress or pitch accent).

Maurer 2008 (apud Bandeira 2017: 258): two level tones H and L (some L better described as neutral), lexical and grammatical function, four melodies on disyllabic nouns (HH mwala, HL plôkô, LH kasô, LL alê); Maurer 2008: 254 concedes tones are not constant. Ferraz 1979: 25 (apud Bandeira and APiCS): no phonologically significant tone; high pitch assigned for stylistic/emphatic effect. Bandeira 2017 judges the tonal hypothesis 'inconsistente' (HL on plôkô mirrors initial stress) and suggests at most a pitch-accent system pending instrumental study.

1637.dq: The critical fact to be obtained from this algorithm is simply that word stress can be predicted from the location of the leftmost high-tone TBU.
1637.dloc: Good 2004 sections 2.3-2.6 (preprint pp. 10, 13-18); Rountree 1972b:26-7 as quoted by Good p.14
1637.heavy: Rountree 1972b (quoted): 'The first long syllable in each foot of the stem is stressed' — Good: '“long syllable” seems to refer to both long vowels... or diphthongs.'
1637.prule: Split lexicon: class (i)-(iii) words are fully specified for H/L tone and show no word stress; the majority class (iv) words carry one lexically placed (contrastive, minimal pairs) pitch-accent mark realized as H tone. In class (iv) words stress is derivable from the accent: the syllable with the leftmost H-tone TBU heads a trochaic foot, the rest of the word is parsed into trochees (no defective foot at the left edge), giving alternating stress. Rountree 1972b's formulation: first long syllable in each foot is stressed, else the penult of the foot.
1637.srule: Accentual words only (tonal words have no stress). tn.quote: Saramaccan, an Atlantic creole spoken in Surinam, has traditionally been analyzed as exhibiting a high-tone/low-tone opposition in its lexicon. However, while it is true that part of its lexicon exhibits a robust high/low opposition, the majority of its words are marked not for tone but pitch accent. The Saramaccan lexicon, therefore, is split with some words being marked for tone and other words marked for accent. ... If one were to examine just this part of the lexicon alone, then Saramaccan would appear to be a language with a rather robust two-tone opposition.

1639.prule: Two-pattern lexical tone/pitch-accent system (nikei akusento): every word belongs to Tone A or Tone B (Hirayama 1951), a lexically specified, synchronically unpredictable class. Tone A = high tone on the penultimate syllable followed by an abrupt fall; Tone B = high tone on the final syllable with no fall. Position is counted in syllables (not moras) from the right edge and the syllable is the tone-bearing unit. Only these two patterns occur regardless of word length. No stress rule is described; the word 'stress' does not occur in the source.

morph.stmt: Gumer 'features the typical root-and-pattern morphology common to all Semitic languages' (§3.1 p.41), with TAM bases formed templatically and person marking on both sides of the base: 'The Perfective receives suffixes only, whereas the Imperfective and Jussive have prefixes and additional suffixes' (§3.11 p.120); objects, possessors, definite articles, future/past and the main-verb marker are suffixed, while negation, causatives (a-, at-), the detransitivizer t(ə)- and the core case relators (yə-, bə-, tə-) are prefixed; nominals take 'a relatively small set of affixes, both prefixes and suffixes' (§4.7 p.242).

1645.prule: Stress is assigned on the 'forma básica' (root, or root + voice suffix): monosyllabic bases are always stressed (with phonetic lengthening and falling pitch); di- and trisyllabic bases are stressed on their second syllable; when suffixes are added, alternate syllables carry stress, iterating rightward from the base stress. Word-level position therefore depends on base size: base-peninitial (word syllable 2, then 4, 6...) for polysyllabic bases, but word-initial (1, 3, 5...) when the base is monosyllabic (yó-wɨ-háʔa̜). Weight plays no role (simple vowel and diphthong monosyllables 'son de la misma duración'). No primary/secondary distinction is drawn among the alternating stresses.
1645.srule: When suffixes are added to the basic form (root, or root + voice suffix), stress falls on alternate syllables counted rightward from the base stress, e.g. /deʔwá-ka-tó-taʔá-de/, /yó-wɨ-háʔa̜/, /hasó-siʔí/ ('las sílabas alternas llevan el acento'). The grammar writes all of a word's stresses with the same acute and does not rank them as primary vs secondary.

1647.heavy: Long vowels/diphthongs bimoraic (heavy); closed syllables heavy by 'weight-by-position' except that the word-final consonant is extrametrical (final CVC = light, final CVVC = heavy); CVCC superheavy with final mora extrametrical. In H H competition vowel length decides: '*LONG-Vunstressed' >> WSP, 'stress is noted only on long vowels (never on short vowels)'. Bashir & Conners 2019: 52 (after Shackle): 'The stressed syllable can be distinguished by having a long vowel, or by the occurrence of a geminated consonant following it'; stress-attracting second syllables are those with a peripheral (long) vowel, V+C, or V+geminate when the first syllable's vowel is centralized (short).
1647.dflt: penult (initial in disyllables `L L; medial in trisyllables L `L L)
1647.prule: One right-aligned moraic trochee per word, built right-to-left, word-final consonant extrametrical. Disyllables: L L -> initial (`pɑ.sɑ); L H and H H with a final long vowel -> final (ʋǝ.`looɽ, sək.`rooɽ, mʊr.`d̪ɑɑr); H + final open/short-vowel syllable -> initial (`us.t̪ri, `khəʈ.ɽɑ). Trisyllables (all CV.CV.C(C)V) -> penult (ɓʊ.`ɦɑ.ri). Net effect: stress the final syllable if it has a long vowel, otherwise the penult; a short vowel/schwa is never stressed when a long vowel is present. Monosyllables always stressed; no secondary stress.
1647.srule: None: 'Words have only one foot: there is no secondary stress' (Atta 2021: 144; abstract p. 129 'secondary stress plays no role here'). Earlier first-hand description differs: Shackle 1976: 28 -- initially-accented trisyllables carry a secondary accent on the third (final) syllable, /"abar'gut/ 'suddenly'; words of more than three syllables are compounds (restated by Bashir & Conners 2019: 52, /ub.baṛ.ˌɣut/).

1648.dq: This section has presented the finding that neither intensity nor duration consistently distinguish major syllables within a word, suggesting that word-level stress is not a feature of Sgaw Karen.
1648.dloc: West 2017: abstract p. ii; sec. 3.2 'Word-level stress' p. 24; sec. 3.6 'Word prosody summary' pp. 32-33. Gilmore 1898: sec. 14 (tones).
1648.prule: No word-level stress. West's acoustic experiment (6 speakers, controlled tone) finds neither intensity nor duration consistently distinguishes major syllables by position within a word; the only word-prosodic asymmetry is major (bimoraic, tone-bearing, full vowel) vs minor (monomoraic, reduced Cə, barred word-finally) syllables. Lexical tone language (Gilmore: six tones per syllable).
1648.srule: Not mentioned in West 2017, secs. 2.1.2, 3.1-3.6 and 5 (pp. 10-11, 20-33, 65-66 read): the source finds no word-level stress at all ('no consistent prominence difference was found for major syllables', p. 65), so no secondary or rhythmic stress is described; a minor+major sequence 'do[es] not form an iamb' (p. 11).
1648.quote: In terms of word prosody, Sgaw Karen does not exhibit word stress cues, but does maintain a prosodic distinction between the more prominent major syllable and the phonologically reduced minor syllable. [p. ii] ... In short, contrary to the stress correlates found in some tonal languages, intensity and duration in Sgaw Karen are not found to correlate to syllable position consistently. Moreover, duration and intensity patterns do not seem linked to the age or sex of the speaker. This section has presented the finding that neither intensity nor duration consistently distinguish major syllables …
1648.loc: West 2017: abstract p. ii; sec. 3.2 'Word-level stress' p. 24; sec. 3.6 'Word prosody summary' pp. 32-33. Gilmore 1898: sec. 14 (tones).
1648.idn: Sgaw Karen (no dialect named; speakers who acquired the language in Karen State, Burma, or Karen refugee camps on the Thai-Burma border); data: Karen culture center, San Diego, California (US diaspora); fieldwork January-March 2017; 12 native speakers aged 18-49 (6 for the word-stress experiment, ages 18-38)

The only stress mention is a quotation of Leslau 1958:146 on a causative formed 'by the change of a stressed syllable into a tone syllable', which Fufa reports 'is not attested' (2009 p.44). Leslau 1958…
morph.elicq: No stress description in the sources read. (For the tone data: 'The researcher used the phonetic analysis program Praat to represent pitch of Shakkinoono.' Fufa 2009 p.4; data are elicited sentences from fieldwork in Masha/Teppi, p.3-4.)

1656.heavy: Lorimer notes only a tendency: 'The stress accent tends to fall on a long vowel, or to lengthen the vowel on which it falls; but this is not an invariable rule.' Not a weight rule.
1656.prule: Word accent is lexically located (one accented syllable/mora per word, position not predictable: disyllables 'usually' initial but 'sometimes' final, polysyllables 'usually' penult but 'sometimes' final, with item-by-item behaviour under suffixation and 'no cast-iron practice'); accent is attracted to long vowels; in verbs certain suffixes (infinitive -o:, transitive preterite -e:/-i:, past participle) always carry the accent (morphological). Modern analysis (Radloff 1999, Schmidt & Kohistani via Baart): stress is assigned lexically to a mora; H tone links to the stressed mora, giving surface high-falling vs low-rising contrast on long vowels (pitch-accent realisation).
1656.srule: A subsidiary (secondary) accent falls 'on the next syllable but one', i.e. two syllables from the main accent, attested both after it (w!alum!usus, secondary on the penult) and before it (am!ušer'e:no); in trisyllables main and subsidiary accent are hard to tell apart (m!u:gul!i). Iteration in longer words not described. Stated by Lorimer 1924 only; the later Gilgit sources opened (Radloff & Shakil 1998 p. 9; Baart c. 2003) speak of one accent per word and do not mention it; Radloff 1999 not openable.

1657.dq: a phonological word in Shǐxīng has a single syllable bearing stress, which is the location for the insertion of lexical tones. The default location of stress is the initial syllable of the domain. ... Both domains (stress domain and tonal domain) coincide in the case of lexical words; the stress domain may be larger than the tonal domain for syntactic phrases.

1657.prule: Word-tone language with no syllable-count or weight-based stress rule. Chirkova 2009 (LTBA): three contrastive tones /H/, /LH/~/L/, /HL/ whose domain is the phonological word; roots lexically specified for tone, affixes toneless. Chirkova & Michaud 2009 analysed the word as carrying one culminative metrical stress, by default on the domain-initial syllable, serving as the anchor for the lexical tone (tone spreads from it; unstressed syllables lose tone; toneless prefixes/proclitics cannot bear stress, so stress shifts right to the first toned syllable; with two toneless prefixes all tones neutralise to L + boundary H). The same author's later primary descriptions (Chirkova & Chen 2013 JIPA; Chirkova 2017 ECLL §2.1.4) explicitly set that autosegmental stress-anchor analysis aside for a 'hybrid' tone/prominence system: two tones on monosyllables (low rising vs high rising) and three lexical melodies on polysyllables, Equal(ly)-Prominent, Left-Prominent, Right-Prominent, the compound melody being predicted by the tone of the leftmost root (high -> LP, rising -> RP). Prominence position is thus part of the lexical tonal melody, not computable from syllable count.
1657.srule: None: 'a phonological word in Shǐxīng has a single syllable bearing stress... one stressed syllable and the remaining unstressed syllables' (Chirkova & Michaud 2009 §4.1); the author's later hybrid tone/prominence descriptions (Chirkova & Chen 2013; Chirkova, Chen & Kocjančič Antolík 2013; Chirkova 2017 §2.1.4) give one EP/LP/RP melody per word and mention no secondary stress.

1657.tone: Chirkova 2009:15-16: 'Shǐxīng is a tonal language. It has three contrastive tones, namely (i) high, /H/, (ii) rising, /LH/, and (iii) falling, /HL/. The domain for tone in Shǐxīng is the phonological word.... Contrastive tone in Shǐxīng is distributed over the word as a whole, irrespective of the number of syllables.... Chirkova & Michaud 2009 treat stress as the tone-bearing anchor (default initial); stress is diagnosed from tone patterns, vowel harmony and reduction of unstressed syllables, not from independent phonetic stress cues. 1659.dq: Each word has a single primary stressed syllable; other syllables have secondary stress. ... 2.3. Stress placement. The position of primary stress in a word is determined.
1659.prule: One primary stress per word; position set by morpheme stress classes: prefixes/infixes never stressed; bare roots stressed; 'retained stress' (strong) roots keep stress unless an inherently stressed suffix is present; 'variably stressed' (weak) roots yield stress to stressable suffixes; suffixes are inherently stressed / inherently unstressed / variably stressed, with a fixed precedence order (reflexive-reciprocal > lexical > instrument > object-actor > voice -m/-xi) among competing stressable suffixes. No syllable-count or weight rule.
1659.srule: Gibson marks two degrees only: 'Each word has a single primary stressed syllable; other syllables have secondary stress' -- his 'secondary stress' (low amplitude, low pitch, unmarked) is the non-primary degree on all remaining syllables; no rhythmic or positional secondary stress is described.

1661.dq: Normally the first syllable of each word is stressed, with alternate following syllables receiving secondary stress.
1661.prule: Contrastive word tone (five lexical stem melodies H, L, HL, LH, HLH; word-tone, melodies spread over suffixes per James 1994). Stress is non-contrastive: by default primary stress on the first syllable of the word, but primary stress also falls on (i) the last H of a run of H tones before an L, (ii) any syllable bearing a contour (glide) tone, (iii) the verb negative suffix -am (with H). Stress placement is thus derivative of the lexical tone pattern with an initial default.
1661.srule: Secondary stress on alternate syllables following the (normally word-initial) primary stress ('Normally the first syllable of each word is stressed, with alternate following syllables receiving secondary stress'); this default pattern can be disturbed by the tone-conditioned primary stresses listed under the primary rule.
1661.quote: Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length) Normally the first syllable of each word is stressed, with alternate following syllables receiving secondary stress. In addition, the final high tone of a series of highs preceding a low tone receives primary stress, a syllable carrying a tone glide receives primary stress, and the verb negative suffix -am is stressed with high tone. There is no contrastive lengthening of either vowels or consonants in any dialect of Siane.
